questions.question: What is a ResultSet in JDBC and how do you iterate it?
questions.title: JDBC ResultSet — Iterating Query Results
questions.direct_answer: A **ResultSet** is a **cursor** over the rows returned by a query. It starts positioned **before the first row**; you call **`next()`** to advance (it returns `false` when rows run out) and `getXxx("col")` to read columns. It's forward-only by default and must be closed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know ResultSet is a cursor and the next()/getXxx iteration loop.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reading a column before calling next(), or assuming it's a loaded list.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note the cursor starts before row 1 and ResultSet is forward-only by default.

sections.title: What a ResultSet Is and How to Iterate
sections.content:
A **`ResultSet`** is a **cursor** (not a loaded list) over the rows a SELECT returns. The cursor begins **before the first row**, so you must call **`next()`** first — it moves to the next row and returns `true`, or `false` when there are no more rows. Inside the loop you read columns with `getInt`, `getString`, etc., by **column name** or **1-based index**.

By default a `ResultSet` is **forward-only** and tied to its `Statement`/`Connection`, so you read it once and **close** it (try-with-resources).

sections.title: ResultSet at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~a cursor|over query rows|not a loaded list|tied to its Statement
emerald|Iterate|~next() loop|starts before row 1|next() returns true/false|getXxx to read
amber|Read columns|~by name or index|getString("name")|getInt(1)|1-based index
rose|Default|~forward-only|read once|close when done|try-with-resources

sections.title: Iterating a ResultSet
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reading before `next()`**: the cursor starts before the first row — always call `next()` first.
- **Treating it as a list**: it's a forward cursor, read once.
- **Using it after closing the Statement/Connection**: the ResultSet becomes invalid.
- **0-based column index**: indices are 1-based (`getInt(1)`).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ResultSet** is a cursor over query rows.
- **Starts before the first row** — call `next()` before reading.
- **`next()`** advances and returns `false` when done.
- **Read** with `getXxx` by column name or 1-based index.
- **Forward-only by default**; close it (try-with-resources).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A ResultSet is a cursor over the rows that a query returns. It's important to understand it's a cursor, not a fully loaded list in memory; it points at one row at a time. The cursor starts positioned before the first row, which is the key detail people forget. So to read data, you first call next, which moves the cursor to the next row and returns true if there's a row there, or false when you've run off the end. That's why the standard pattern is a while loop on rs dot next. Inside the loop, you read each column with the typed getters, like getInt and getString, and you can read either by column name, which is more readable, or by a one-based column index. By default a ResultSet is forward-only, meaning you iterate through it once from start to finish, and it's tied to the Statement and Connection that produced it, so once those are closed the ResultSet is invalid. That's why you close it when you're done, ideally with try-with-resources. The mistakes to avoid are trying to read a column before calling next, since the cursor starts before the first row, treating the ResultSet like a reusable list, and using zero-based column indices when they're actually one-based.

questions.question: How do you check for NULL values when reading from a ResultSet?
questions.title: Checking NULL Values in JDBC ResultSet
questions.direct_answer: Numeric getters like `getInt`/`getLong` return **0** for a SQL NULL, which is ambiguous. To detect a real NULL, call **`rs.wasNull()`** right after the getter, or use **`getObject`** (which returns Java `null`). This distinguishes 'value is 0' from 'value is missing'.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know primitive getters return 0 for NULL and how to detect it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating a returned 0/false as a real value when the column was NULL.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use wasNull() immediately after the read, or getObject for nullable columns.

sections.title: Checking for NULL in a ResultSet
sections.content:
JDBC's primitive getters can't represent NULL: **`getInt`/`getLong`/`getDouble` return 0** and `getBoolean` returns `false` when the column is SQL **NULL** — indistinguishable from a real 0 or false. To tell them apart:

- Call **`rs.wasNull()`** **immediately after** the getter — it reports whether the last read column was NULL.
- Or use **`getObject(col)`** / wrapper-returning getters, which return Java **`null`** for a NULL.

For object getters like `getString`, a NULL already comes back as `null`, so this mainly matters for primitives.

sections.title: NULL in ResultSet at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|Primitive getters|~0 for NULL|getInt -> 0|getBoolean -> false|ambiguous
blue|wasNull()|~the check|call right after getter|true if last read was NULL|positional
emerald|getObject|~returns null|Integer / null|clean for nullable cols|preferred
amber|String getters|~already null|getString -> null|no wasNull needed|

sections.title: Ambiguous: 0 might be a real value or NULL
Clear: use wasNull() or getObject
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Trusting a returned 0/false**: it may be a NULL, not a real value.
- **Calling `wasNull()` too late**: it refers to the *last* column read — call it right after.
- **Mapping nullable columns to primitives**: use wrappers/`getObject`.
- **Forgetting `getString` returns null**: object getters already handle NULL.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Primitive getters return 0/false** for SQL NULL — ambiguous.
- **`rs.wasNull()`** (right after the getter) detects a NULL read.
- **`getObject`** returns Java `null` for NULL — cleaner for nullable columns.
- **`getString`** already returns `null` for NULL.
- **Don't map nullable columns** to primitives.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Checking for NULL in a ResultSet matters because JDBC's primitive getters can't actually represent a NULL. If a numeric column is SQL NULL, getInt and getLong return zero, getDouble returns zero point zero, and getBoolean returns false. The problem is that's indistinguishable from a genuine zero or false in the data, so you can't tell whether the value was really zero or was actually missing. There are two clean ways to handle this. The first is to call rs dot wasNull immediately after the getter; it reports whether the last column you read was NULL. The key detail is that wasNull refers to the most recent read, so you have to call it right after the getter, before reading anything else. The second, and usually cleaner, approach is to use getObject, which returns a Java object that's null when the column is NULL, so you can just check for null. For object-returning getters like getString, this isn't an issue, because getString already returns null for a NULL column; the ambiguity only affects the primitive getters. So my practice is to never map a nullable column to a primitive; I either check wasNull right after the read or use getObject, so I can clearly distinguish a real zero from a missing value.

questions.question: How do you map ResultSet rows to Java objects in JDBC?
questions.title: Mapping ResultSet to Java Objects in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: To map a `ResultSet` to Java objects, iterate it and for each row read the columns and construct your object — typically inside a reusable **RowMapper** (`ResultSet → T`). This keeps mapping logic in one place; Spring's `JdbcTemplate` formalizes the same pattern.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can convert rows into domain objects cleanly.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Inlining mapping everywhere, duplicating column reads and bugs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Extract a RowMapper; mention Spring JdbcTemplate uses exactly this abstraction.

sections.title: Mapping ResultSet Rows to Objects
sections.content:
Database rows are flat columns; your app wants **objects**. The pattern: loop with `next()`, read each column, and build a domain object per row, collecting them into a `List`. To avoid duplicating that read-and-construct logic, extract it into a **RowMapper** — a small function `ResultSet -> T` that maps one row.

This is exactly the abstraction **Spring's `JdbcTemplate`** uses (`RowMapper<T>`), letting you write the mapping once and reuse it across queries.

sections.title: Row Mapping at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Pattern|~loop + build|next() per row|read columns|construct object
emerald|RowMapper|~ResultSet -> T|one place for mapping|reusable|testable
amber|Collect|~into a List|add per row|return list|or Optional for one
rose|Spring|~same idea|JdbcTemplate RowMapper|query(sql, mapper)|less boilerplate

sections.title: Mapping Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | run query → `ResultSet` |
| 2 | `while (rs.next())` |
| 3 | read columns, build object |
| 4 | add to `List<T>`, return |

sections.title: A reusable RowMapper
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Inlining mapping everywhere**: duplicates column reads; extract a RowMapper.
- **Column name typos**: a wrong name throws at runtime — keep mapping centralized.
- **Ignoring NULLs**: use `getObject`/`wasNull` for nullable columns.
- **Building objects before `next()`**: read only after advancing the cursor.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Loop** with `next()`, read columns, build an object per row.
- **Extract a RowMapper** (`ResultSet -> T`) for reuse.
- **Collect** into a `List<T>` (or `Optional<T>` for one).
- **Spring `JdbcTemplate`** uses the same `RowMapper` pattern.
- **Handle NULLs** with `getObject`/`wasNull`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Mapping a ResultSet to Java objects is about turning flat database columns into your domain objects. The basic pattern is to loop with next, and for each row read the columns and construct an object, adding each one to a list that you return. That works, but if you inline that read-and-construct logic in every query, you end up duplicating column reads and it's easy to introduce bugs. So the cleaner approach is to extract a RowMapper, which is just a small function that takes a ResultSet positioned on a row and returns one object of your type, a ResultSet to T mapping. You write the mapping once and reuse it across queries, which also makes it easy to test. For example, I'd define a User record and a userMapper lambda that reads id, name, and email from the current row and builds a User, then in my query loop I just call the mapper for each row. This is exactly the abstraction Spring's JdbcTemplate provides with its RowMapper interface; you pass a RowMapper to jdbcTemplate dot query and it handles the iteration for you, so you write far less boilerplate. A couple of things to keep in mind while mapping: centralize it to avoid column-name typos scattered everywhere, and for nullable columns use getObject or check wasNull so you handle NULLs correctly instead of getting a default value.

questions.question: What happens if you do not close a ResultSet in JDBC?
questions.title: Consequences of Not Closing ResultSet in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: An unclosed `ResultSet` leaks resources — it holds a **database cursor** and memory on both client and server. Leaks accumulate and can exhaust cursors/connections, eventually causing errors or hangs. The fix is **try-with-resources**, which closes the `ResultSet` automatically, even on exceptions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know unclosed ResultSets leak cursors and the try-with-resources fix.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying on Statement/Connection close or GC to clean up the ResultSet.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note closing the Statement closes its ResultSet, but explicit try-with-resources is clearest.

sections.title: What Happens If You Don't Close a ResultSet
sections.content:
A `ResultSet` holds real resources: a **database cursor** on the server and buffers on the client. If you don't close it, those resources aren't released promptly — a **leak**. Under load, leaked cursors accumulate until you hit the database's **open-cursor limit** or exhaust connections, causing errors or hangs.

Closing a `Statement` or `Connection` does close its `ResultSet`, but relying on that (or on garbage collection, which is non-deterministic) is fragile. The robust fix is **try-with-resources**: declare the `ResultSet` in the `try(...)` and it closes automatically, even if an exception is thrown.

sections.title: Unclosed ResultSet at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|Leak|~holds resources|DB cursor + buffers|not released|accumulates
blue|Symptom|~under load|open-cursor limit hit|errors/hangs|hard to spot in tests
amber|GC not enough|~non-deterministic|don't rely on it|close explicitly|
emerald|Fix|~try-with-resources|auto-close|even on exception|reverse order

sections.title: Leak-prone: ResultSet not closed on error
Safe: try-with-resources closes the ResultSet
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Unclosed ResultSet** leaks a DB cursor + client buffers.
- **Leaks accumulate** → hit open-cursor limits → errors/hangs.
- **GC is non-deterministic** — don't rely on it.
- **Closing the Statement** closes its ResultSet, but be explicit.
- **try-with-resources** closes it safely, even on exceptions.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: If you don't close a ResultSet, you leak resources, because a ResultSet holds a real database cursor on the server side plus buffers on the client side. When you fail to close it, those resources aren't released promptly. One unclosed ResultSet won't hurt, but under load they accumulate, and eventually you can hit the database's limit on the number of open cursors, or exhaust connections, which shows up as errors or the application hanging. It's a sneaky bug because it's invisible with a couple of rows in a test and only surfaces under real traffic. Now, technically, closing the Statement or the Connection will also close any ResultSet it produced, so people sometimes rely on that. But relying on it is fragile, and relying on garbage collection is worse, because GC is non-deterministic and the cursor could stay open for a long time. The robust fix is try-with-resources: you declare the ResultSet, and ideally the PreparedStatement too, in the parentheses of the try, and Java guarantees they're closed automatically when the block exits, in reverse order, even if an exception is thrown in the middle of processing. That makes the cleanup deterministic and removes the leak entirely, which is why I always use try-with-resources for ResultSets.

beats.text: Every open ResultSet holds a server-side cursor. That cursor eats database memory and counts toward the server's open-cursor limit. Skip the close and it lingers. It stays open until the connection closes or the database times it out.
Why does closing matter so much? A ResultSet isn't just a Java object. It maps to a live cursor the database server tracks. Closing tells that server to free the cursor's resources right away.

items: Unclosed ResultSet. The server cursor stays open and keeps eating memory on the database.
Cursor limit hit. Oracle throws ORA-01000 for too many open cursors, and MySQL caps it too.
Implicit close chain. Closing a Statement closes its ResultSets, but leaning on that stays risky.
try-with-resources. It closes the ResultSet, then the Statement, in reverse order on its own.

beats.text: Say a method fetches orders but an exception jumps out before the close. That server cursor stays open. Repeat it under load and a hundred leaked cursors pile up. Soon you trip a max-open-cursors error. Here's the non-obvious part. try-with-resources on the ResultSet frees the cursor no matter what exception flies.

items: Trusting Connection close to clean up. It works late, but the cursor sits open the whole time.
Assuming JPA makes this moot. Hibernate opens JDBC result sets too, and bad lazy loading leaves them open.

speakable_v2.cap: So always close result sets on purpose. try-with-resources is the safest one-line way to guarantee it.
